The contention that a Woman Suffrage amendment should not come before the United States Congress was agaim discussed toward the close of the hearing by Mrs. Carrie Chapman Catt. Mrs. Catt said

“We are going to stand by our rights to get the vote by Federal amendment. It is as easy a problem as it was to give enfranchisement to the negro, and while there are gentlemen from the South who do not think this was done in a conservative way, nevertheless it has stood the test of some forty years and is stil a part of our Constitution.”

In the course of the hearing Mr. Henry asked Dr. Shaw if the National Association would be satisfied if the Committee on the Election of President, Vice-President, and Representatives in Congress were given jurisdiction over the question of Woman Suffrage also. Dr. Shaw, after consultation with the National Board, said emphatically “No." The Committee on the Election of President, Vice-president, and Representatives in Congress, Dr. Shaw stated, would also be a very busy one in the coming session, since the question of presidential primaries urged by President Wilson in his message to Congress would come in due course to this committee. Suffragists would gair no jot of advantage by the trans ference of their question from one busy committee to another.

Miss Alice Edith Abell, president of the Wage Earners' AntiSuffrage Association of New York City, said

“If the ballot would benefit any women, those most to benefit would be the working women, and they are the ones who do not want the ballot. They know that they would lose more than they would gain. Whenever women become equal with men before the law, which they would be if allowed to vote, they will lose all protective legislation which has been granted them because they are not equal legally

ing of the Forty-fifth Convention of the National Woman Suffrage Association, assembled in the Columbia Theater on November 30, 1913, Dr. Anna Howard Shaw, President, in the chair, calls upon the President of the United States in his forthcoming message to Congress to
December 6, 1913

“The wage-earning woman already has more of the responsibilities of man's life than she wants. She has found herself unequal in many ways to discharge the masculine responsibilities which her industrial independence has brought her. She has all and more than she can satisfactorily attend to, and she objects to having more thrust upon her.”

At the rebuttal the following day Miss Alice Stone Blackwell, Mrs. Catherine Waugh McCullough, Mrs. Ida Husted Harper, Mrs. William Kent, Mrs. John Rogers, Jr., Mrs. Thomas Hepburn, Representative T. W. Mondell, Mrs. Solon Jacobs, Mrs. Baldridge, Mrs. Oscar Huntley, Mrs. French of Tennessee, Mrs. Wester of Tennessee, Miss Helen Todd, of California, and others spoke. The rebuttal was extremely pointed and witty. The committee will announce its decision later.
